topics.title: What an actor actually does
topics.lesson_markdown: An actor does more than display emotion. In a scripted scene, the actor makes purposeful choices **under imagined circumstances** while remaining responsive to partners and camera. Compare two deliveries of “You came back”: one as a polite greeting, one as a concealed accusation. The words do not change; objectives, pauses, gaze and breath do. The audience reads behavior, not the actor's private explanation. **Demonstrate:** record both deliveries in identical framing. **Pitfall:** playing “anger” as a facial mask. **Practice:** invent three playable intentions for the line; have a partner identify the intention without being told. **Evidence:** purposeful physical/vocal change and credible response.

topics.title: Set etiquette and consent
topics.lesson_markdown: A film set is a coordinated workplace. The actor takes direction from the director through agreed set channels, respects the first AD's schedule, maintains quiet during rolling, knows the route for safety concerns, and does not touch another performer or change physical choreography without agreement. “Action” begins the take, but a safety concern can stop it. Learn call sheet essentials: time, location, scenes, transport, emergency contact and required wardrobe. **Demonstrate:** a safe call-time-to-wrap walkthrough. **Pitfall:** treating urgency as permission to bypass a safety protocol. **Practice:** read a sample call sheet and identify an unsafe change; report it through the right channel. **Evidence:** accurate briefing and boundary-setting.

topics.title: Script reading and factual analysis
topics.lesson_markdown: On first read, separate facts **explicitly in the script** from ideas the actor invents. Mark scene heading (INT/EXT, place, time), action lines, character cues and dialogue. Record what is known about relationships, timing, location and events just before the scene. Ask: what changes by the end? Avoid deciding how to say every line before you understand the sequence. **Demonstrate:** annotate a two-page family-conflict scene. **Pitfall:** mistaking an inferred backstory for an established script fact. **Practice:** produce a fact/inference table with evidence line references. **Evidence:** coherent given circumstances.

topics.title: Objective, obstacle and stakes
topics.lesson_markdown: An **objective** is what the character wants from someone now, expressible with an active verb such as persuade, hide, protect or confront. An **obstacle** resists that wish. **Stakes** explain why the outcome matters. In a Lagos apartment dispute, “be sad” is not an actionable objective; “convince my landlord to give me another week” is. Strong scene work tracks what a character does when the first tactic fails. **Demonstrate:** same lines with low and high stakes. **Pitfall:** confusing the actor's preferred emotion with the character's target. **Practice:** write a “I want X from Y before Z, but…” statement. **Evidence:** partner-directed action with visible stakes.

topics.title: Beats and tactics
topics.lesson_markdown: A **beat** is a meaningful change in intention, information, action or relationship within a scene. A **tactic** is what the character tries to obtain the objective: flatter, bargain, threaten, confess. When the partner refuses, the actor can change tactics without changing the scene's overall goal. Mark beats at a shift in action rather than at every punctuation mark. **Demonstrate:** a mother persuading a daughter to stay home, first by joking, then revealing a secret. **Pitfall:** playing every line with identical force. **Practice:** mark three turning points and perform each with a different playable tactic. **Evidence:** readable causal shifts.

topics.title: Given circumstances and subtext
topics.lesson_markdown: **Given circumstances** are concrete facts: who, where, when, events and relationships. **Subtext** is the meaning or intention beneath the spoken words. “The food is getting cold” may really mean “Please stop avoiding our argument,” depending on evidence in the scene. Subtext should sharpen behavior, not become a secret essay viewers cannot see. **Demonstrate:** kitchen dialogue with and without a concealed grievance. **Pitfall:** inventing subtext that contradicts explicit circumstances. **Practice:** add subtext notes to four lines, then show them through looks and pauses. **Evidence:** a partner can infer the concealed need.

topics.title: Imagination and healthy emotion
topics.lesson_markdown: Emotion can emerge from attention, objectives, imagery, physical action and partner interaction. No student must recount trauma or force distress to achieve an authentic take. A performer can build safe fictional specifics, a sensory environment and actionable stakes, then exit the role with grounding and de-roling. **Demonstrate:** a worried parent scene through attentive listening rather than forced tears. **Pitfall:** using personal psychological harm as a shortcut. **Practice:** devise two safe imaginary circumstances and a post-scene reset. **Evidence:** repeatable, bounded emotional availability.

topics.title: Listening and reactions
topics.lesson_markdown: On screen, a reaction can carry more story than a speech. A listening actor observes the partner, absorbs new information, and allows it to alter timing, body and intention. Listening is an active task, even when the actor has no lines. In a two-shot and close-up, compare waiting for a cue with genuinely processing the announcement “I sold the house.” **Pitfall:** rehearsing your next line mentally. **Practice:** shoot the same exchange twice with a changed, unknown partner choice. **Evidence:** responses genuinely track the stimulus.

topics.title: Physicality and status
topics.lesson_markdown: Posture, space, movement tempo and gesture can express occupation, age, health, status or emotional pressure without caricature. External choices must arise from character and social situation, not stereotypes about class or disability. **Demonstrate:** who controls space during a job interview; adjust a chair and eyeline. **Pitfall:** fidgeting to signal “nervous.” **Practice:** perform identical dialogue with two different status relationships. **Evidence:** purposeful and consistent physical choices.

topics.title: Voice and dialogue clarity
topics.lesson_markdown: Support clear speech with relaxed breath and unforced articulation. Camera dialogue rarely needs stage projection when a boom/lavalier is correctly placed. Anger or whispers must remain intelligible without shouting or vocal strain. Observe consonant clarity, pace, breath groups and the mic placement plan. **Demonstrate:** noisy roadside dialogue recorded with and without vocal discipline. **Pitfall:** tightening the throat for intensity. **Practice:** read an 80-word monologue at three dynamics while keeping meaning intelligible. **Evidence:** clear consonants, sustainable voice, stable level.

topics.title: Language and accent ethics
topics.lesson_markdown: Nollywood performance draws from English, Nigerian Pidgin and many African languages. Language choice signals home, community, intimacy, power and identity. Obtain pronunciation coaching and speaker review; document whether code-switching is written or improvised. An accent should be credible to character and region, not a joke unless the story intentionally and responsibly critiques it. **Demonstrate:** the same request to a parent, a friend and an employer. **Pitfall:** flattening communities into stock accents. **Practice:** build a pronunciation and code-switching sheet with a competent speaker. **Evidence:** clear intention and respectful consistency.

topics.title: Shot size and performance scale
topics.lesson_markdown: A close-up magnifies small changes around eyes, mouth and breath; a wide shot communicates spatial behavior and relationship. The useful question is not “do less always,” but “what must the audience read at this distance?” Match performance energy to the dramatic event while calibrating size and physical continuity. **Demonstrate:** one revelation in wide, medium and close-up. **Pitfall:** overacting facial expression in tight framing or becoming inert in a wide. **Practice:** adapt the same beat to three shot sizes. **Evidence:** clear objective in all three.

topics.title: Eyelines and screen direction
topics.lesson_markdown: Actors usually look at an agreed off-camera eyeline near, not into, the lens unless the script/design calls for direct address. An established axis helps maintain consistent screen direction in a conversation, though directors may cross it intentionally with clear visual motivation. Performance must stay with the partner while respecting the camera/eyeline plan. **Demonstrate:** diagram the axis for two actors at a table; compare wrong and right eyelines in edit. **Pitfall:** following the moving camera with one's gaze. **Practice:** mark eyelines and shoot matching singles. **Evidence:** edit preserves audience geography.

topics.title: Blocking and continuity
topics.lesson_markdown: **Blocking** is planned movement in relation to partners, props and camera. A **mark** helps focus, lighting and composition. Continuity includes which hand lifts a cup, line timing, standing position and eyeline; the actor stays flexible when a director changes coverage. **Demonstrate:** same action across wide, over-shoulder and close-up. **Pitfall:** changing the gesture/prop hand between takes. **Practice:** make a continuity log from three takes and match a specific gesture. **Evidence:** cuts preserve movement and intention.

topics.title: Self-tape auditions
topics.lesson_markdown: A strong self-tape prioritizes readable face, clear voice, neutral uncluttered background, correct framing, good light, controlled eyeline and following casting instructions. Respect file naming, slate requirements, deadlines, character context and privacy. Do not add distracting graphics or expensive equipment for its own sake. **Demonstrate:** poor and improved mobile-phone submissions. **Pitfall:** talking to the lens when a partner eyeline was requested. **Practice:** submit a named 60–90-second tape with self-evaluation. **Evidence:** casting-ready technical and creative quality.

topics.title: Cold reads
topics.lesson_markdown: A cold read is not a memory test. Quickly identify the relationship, turning point, objective and immediate stakes, then read with connection to partner and text. Prioritize comprehension over accent tricks or a fully fixed emotional result. When permitted, ask one concise, useful clarification question. **Demonstrate:** a 90-second preparation of unfamiliar sides. **Pitfall:** staring at the script through the partner's lines. **Practice:** prepare a short surprise scene with a timer. **Evidence:** coherent intention and responsive reading.

topics.title: Improvisation and offers
topics.lesson_markdown: Improvisation requires listening, accepting a playable offer, and advancing the scene with specific action. “Yes, and” means build cooperatively, not agree with harmful actions or surrender personal boundaries. Structure improv with where, relationship, objective and change. **Demonstrate:** a market-stall misunderstanding, then repeat with a new offer. **Pitfall:** blocking every partner idea or chasing jokes without stakes. **Practice:** improvise a one-minute conflict in a familiar local setting. **Evidence:** clear jointly built story.

topics.title: Ensemble rhythm
topics.lesson_markdown: Dialogue rhythm depends on thought, subtext, listening and editing needs. Overlap can convey pressure or intimacy, but uncontrolled overlap may make recording and coverage difficult. Silence must carry activity, not emptiness. **Demonstrate:** family-dinner argument played once with pauses, once with controlled overlap; assess clarity in edit. **Pitfall:** a mechanically timed pause with no character reason. **Practice:** coordinate breath/overlap points with sound and director. **Evidence:** emotionally clear but cuttable sequence.

topics.title: Comedy and timing
topics.lesson_markdown: Comedy often arises from a precise character objective meeting a frustrating obstacle. The performer may commit seriously to absurd circumstances rather than “announce the joke.” Set-up, expectation, reveal, reaction and edit duration all shape timing. Cultural humor needs context and care around marginalized identities. **Demonstrate:** two versions of a misdelivered parcel gag. **Pitfall:** laughing at one's own line or forcing mugging for camera. **Practice:** build a 30-second visual-comedy scene with no dialogue. **Evidence:** audience understands the reversal.

topics.title: High-intensity drama safely
topics.lesson_markdown: Grief, fear and conflict can be built from truthful objectives, safe substitution, breath, scene partners and repeatable physical actions. The director and student agree beforehand on physical boundaries, break cues and off-ramps. Repeated screaming or forced crying is not a quality metric. **Demonstrate:** a family-loss scene with controlled intensification and recovery. **Pitfall:** confusing exhaustion with emotional truth. **Practice:** record an intense beat twice, then use a short de-role routine. **Evidence:** consistent emotional story and wellbeing.

topics.title: Intimacy and consent
topics.lesson_markdown: Scenes involving nudity, simulated sex or other sensitive intimacy require clear advance discussion, specific consent, defined choreography and a qualified intimacy professional where applicable. Students may decline an exercise without academic retaliation; provide equivalent competencies through non-intimate scenes. Consent is ongoing and can be withdrawn. Never request learner nudity or improvised intimate touching. **Demonstrate:** fully clothed, non-intimate boundary negotiation and camera cheat. **Pitfall:** treating an earlier yes as blanket approval. **Practice:** document a fictional scene's boundaries, closure and escalation contact. **Evidence:** precise consent communication.

topics.title: Stunt-aware acting
topics.lesson_markdown: An actor sells danger through reaction, eyeline, timing and edited coverage while specialists control the actual hazard. Only qualified personnel design and supervise stunts, weapons, vehicles, falls and fight choreography. A student may rehearse a harmless camera-angle illusion but must never stage actual strikes or dangerous falls. **Demonstrate:** implied impact using separate actor reaction and sound effect, with no contact. **Pitfall:** “making it realistic” with real impact. **Practice:** plan a zero-contact confrontation and risk checklist. **Evidence:** believable edit with no real hazard.

topics.title: Design and continuity collaboration
topics.lesson_markdown: Wardrobe silhouettes, fabrics, makeup continuity, personal props and physical environment tell character history. The performer should know what each prop means, how it is handled and what changes between scenes. In a hospital/office set, accuracy depends on approved reference and technical advisers, not the actor inventing clinical behavior or confidential data. **Demonstrate:** continuity photo board and three takes with a handbag or medical chart prop. **Pitfall:** changing a costume/prop action unlogged. **Practice:** create a character look-and-prop continuity sheet. **Evidence:** defensible story choice and matched takes.

topics.title: ADR, reel and career
topics.lesson_markdown: **ADR** replaces or supplements recorded dialogue while matching timing, emotion and acoustics. **Pickups** collect missing shots or lines that support the edit. A strong actor reel opens with a clear, recent, well-shot moment, gives accurate credit, uses only cleared footage and removes filler. Learn release terms, agent/manager distinction, safe audition reporting and transparent professional expectations. **Demonstrate:** align a short ADR line to picture and cut a concise reel. **Pitfall:** placing copyrighted uncleared scenes or misleading credits in a public reel. **Practice:** submit a 60–90-second permissions-checked reel and a career plan. **Evidence:** credible, ethical, accessible portfolio.
